options: Because the writer made a mistake
Because ὃ is the object of δώσω, as expected, and οὗ is genitive by attraction to ὕδατος
Because the two clauses have different verbs
Because οὗ is plural and ὃ is singular
items.explain: Both would normally be accusative, the object of δώσω. In the first clause the relative has been drawn into the genitive of its antecedent ὕδατος, which follows ἐκ. The verbs are the same, and both pronouns are singular.

options: The order is random and has no effect
The predicate θεός stands before the verb, which is often read as giving it prominence

The subject ὁ λόγος is first, which makes it the topic
items.explain: θεός comes first in the clause, and ὁ λόγος, with the article, follows the verb. Many grammarians read the fronting as a way of giving the predicate prominence. Word order is a clue and not a proof; the cases show which word is the subject.

options: Because a genitive pronoun can never be the subject of a participle
Because λαλοῦντος is in the nominative
Because the participle has an article
Because the verb Ἀκηκόαμεν governs the genitive: 'we have heard him speaking'
items.explain: A verb of hearing often takes the genitive of the person heard, so αὐτοῦ is linked to the main verb, and λαλοῦντος tells what he was doing. options: It is a relative clause that modifies οὐρανός
It is a time clause, 'until heaven and earth pass away', that modifies οὐ μὴ παρέλθῃ
It is a purpose clause: 'in order that heaven pass away'
It is the content clause of a verb of saying
items.explain: ἕως ἂν with the subjunctive opens a clause of time, 'until'. It is subordinate to the main verb of the other half of the sentence, οὐ μὴ παρέλθῃ, a strong denial. The second ἕως ἂν clause, near the end, is a time clause of the same kind. It has no relative pronoun, so it does not modify a noun.
